options.label: The Earth turning on its axis
options.feedback: One turn carries you through light and dark.

options.label: The Earth circling the Sun
options.feedback: That takes a year and gives the seasons.

options.label: The Sun switching off at night
options.feedback: The Sun shines without pause.

options.label: The Moon blocking the Sun
options.feedback: That is an eclipse, and it is rare and brief.

items.ok_line: Night is simply your side of the planet facing away.
items.ko_line: One of these happens once a day. The others do not.
items.exp_text: The Earth turns once in about 24 hours, carrying every place through sunlight and then through its own shadow. Half the planet is always lit and half always dark; sunrise and sunset are simply you crossing the boundary between them. At the equator that boundary sweeps past at about 1,670 km/h, which is how fast you are travelling east while sitting still.

items.prompt: Which way does the Earth turn?

options.label: Eastward
options.feedback: Which is why the Sun appears to rise in the east.

options.label: Westward
options.feedback: Then the Sun would rise in the west.

options.label: It changes with the seasons
options.feedback: The direction has never changed.

options.label: Northward, along its axis
options.feedback: A body cannot spin along its own axis.

items.ok_line: You turn east, so everything in the sky appears to rise there.
items.ko_line: Work backwards from where the Sun comes up.
items.exp_title: Everything rises in the east because we turn east
items.exp_text: The Earth spins eastward, so any fixed point is carried towards the Sun in the morning and away from it in the evening. Everything in the sky follows the same rule — the Moon, the planets and the stars all appear to rise in the east and set in the west, because none of them is really moving that way. On Venus the spin is reversed, and the Sun there rises in the west.

items.prompt: How long does the Earth take to turn once relative to the stars?

options.label: Just under 24 hours
options.feedback: 23 hours and 56 minutes, four minutes short of a day.

options.label: Exactly 24 hours
options.feedback: That is the turn relative to the Sun, not the stars.

options.label: Just over 25 hours
options.feedback: Nothing in the day runs that long.

options.label: 12 hours
options.feedback: That is roughly one half-turn.

items.ok_line: Four minutes short, and those four minutes explain the whole year.
items.ko_line: The Earth also moves along its orbit while turning. That costs a little extra.
items.exp_title: Two kinds of day, four minutes apart
items.exp_text: One full turn against the stars takes 23 h 56 min. But the Earth has also travelled a little along its orbit, so it must turn about a degree further to bring the Sun back overhead — hence the 24-hour solar day. Those four minutes accumulate: stars rise four minutes earlier each night, two hours earlier each month, and a whole cycle across the year, which is why the constellations change with the season.

items.prompt: Why is it not the same time everywhere on Earth at once?

options.label: The Sun is overhead at different places
options.feedback: Noon arrives westward as the planet turns.

options.label: Clocks run at different rates
options.feedback: A second is the same length everywhere.

options.label: The Sun moves across the sky unevenly
options.feedback: Its apparent motion is nearly constant.

options.label: Light takes time to cross the Earth
options.feedback: It crosses the planet in a tenth of a second.

items.ok_line: Noon is a place as much as a moment.
items.ko_line: Ask when the Sun is highest for you, and when it is highest for someone far east.
items.exp_text: Noon is the moment the Sun stands highest, and that moment reaches each meridian in turn as the planet rotates, sweeping westward around the globe. Two towns a few hundred kilometres apart genuinely have noon at different instants. Every town once kept its own time by the Sun, and it worked perfectly well until railways made it impossible to write a timetable.

items.prompt: Where does the Sun stay above the horizon for months at a time?

options.label: Inside the polar circles
options.feedback: The tilt keeps those regions lit all summer.

options.label: At the equator
options.feedback: There the day is close to twelve hours all year.

options.label: On the highest mountains
options.feedback: Height buys minutes, not months.

options.label: In the middle of the oceans
options.feedback: The sea follows the same rules as the land.

items.ok_line: Far enough north or south, the Sun stops setting altogether.
items.ko_line: It depends on latitude, and on the tilt of the Earth's axis.
items.exp_title: The Sun that will not set
items.exp_text: The Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees, so in summer the pole leans towards the Sun and regions inside the polar circle stay lit as the planet turns — the Sun circles the sky without touching the horizon. At the pole itself this lasts about six months, followed by six months of night. The far north and south get the same total daylight per year as anywhere else, delivered in two enormous instalments.

items.prompt: Why is the sky dark at night if there are billions of stars?

options.label: They are unimaginably far away
options.feedback: Brightness falls off steeply with distance.

options.label: Most stars are switched off at night
options.feedback: Stars shine continuously.

options.label: The Earth's shadow blocks them
options.feedback: That shadow is what makes night, and stars are outside it.

options.label: The Moon outshines them all
options.feedback: The sky is still dark on a moonless night.

items.ok_line: Distance, and a universe that has not been around forever.
items.ko_line: The stars are there. Ask why so little of their light arrives.
items.exp_text: If the universe were infinite, unchanging and eternally old, every line of sight would end on a star and the whole sky would blaze. That it does not is called Olbers' paradox, and the resolution is that the universe has a finite age — light from the most distant regions has not had time to arrive — and expansion has stretched much of what does arrive out of the visible range. The darkness of the night sky is evidence that the universe began.

items.prompt: Why do the stars appear to wheel around one point in the sky?

options.label: The Earth turns beneath them
options.feedback: That point lies on the axis you are spinning around.

options.label: The stars orbit that point
options.feedback: They are far too distant to circle anything nearby.

options.label: The sky rotates as a solid shell
options.feedback: There is no shell. The stars lie at every distance.

options.label: The atmosphere drags them round
options.feedback: Air cannot move objects light-years away.

items.ok_line: You are on a turning platform, and that point is your axle.
items.ko_line: Nothing up there is moving in a circle. Something down here is turning.
items.exp_title: Looking straight up your own axis
items.exp_text: The Earth's axis points at a fixed spot among the stars, and everything appears to circle it because you are the one rotating. In the north that spot happens to be marked by Polaris, which barely moves all night and stands at an altitude equal to your latitude — a fact that let sailors find their position for centuries. The southern sky has no bright equivalent.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon show the same face to us at all times?

options.label: It turns once per orbit
options.feedback: Its spin and its orbit take exactly the same time.

options.label: It does not turn at all
options.feedback: Then we would see every side of it in turn.

options.label: The far side is always dark
options.feedback: The far side gets as much sunlight as the near one.

options.label: Earth's shadow hides the far side
options.feedback: The shadow reaches it only during an eclipse.

items.ok_line: It does turn — at exactly the rate that keeps one face towards us.
items.ko_line: Walk around a chair while always facing it. Did you turn?
items.exp_text: The Moon rotates once every 27.3 days, exactly the time it takes to orbit, so the same hemisphere always faces us. This is not coincidence: Earth's gravity raised a bulge on the Moon and slowly braked its spin until the two periods matched, a state called tidal locking that is common among moons. The far side is not dark — it gets the same sunlight, just never while we are watching.

items.prompt: What is happening when the Moon is visible in the daytime sky?

options.label: It is simply above the horizon
options.feedback: It rises and sets on its own schedule, day or night.

options.label: Something has gone wrong
options.feedback: It is entirely ordinary, and happens most months.

options.label: It is closer than usual
options.feedback: Distance has nothing to do with when it is up.

options.label: It is being eclipsed
options.feedback: An eclipse is a different event altogether.

items.ok_line: Nothing unusual. It was always going to be up at some point.
items.ko_line: The Moon keeps its own timetable, and it does not consult the Sun.
items.exp_title: The Moon keeps its own hours
items.exp_text: The Moon rises about fifty minutes later each day as it moves along its orbit, so it spends part of each month above the horizon during daylight. A first-quarter Moon rises around noon and is high in the afternoon sky. It looks pale because the daytime sky is bright, not because the Moon is faint. Only the full Moon is reliably a night-time object, since being opposite the Sun it rises as the Sun sets.

items.prompt: Why does a day on Earth grow very slightly longer over time?

options.label: The tides are braking the spin
options.feedback: Friction from the ocean bulge slows the Earth.

options.label: The Earth is getting heavier
options.feedback: Its mass is very nearly constant.

options.label: The Sun is pulling harder
options.feedback: The Sun's pull is essentially unchanged.

options.label: The atmosphere is thickening
options.feedback: Air has no grip on the planet's rotation.

items.ok_line: The Moon is dragging on our oceans, and it costs us spin.
items.ko_line: Something raises a bulge of water that the turning Earth has to drag around.
items.exp_title: The Moon is slowing us down
items.exp_text: The Moon raises a tidal bulge in the oceans, and the turning Earth drags that bulge slightly ahead of it. The friction costs the Earth rotation — about 1.7 milliseconds per century — and the energy is handed to the Moon, which drifts some 3.8 cm further away each year. Fossil corals record daily growth bands showing that a year once held around 400 days. Both effects were measured directly with mirrors left on the lunar surface.
